Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. - artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. The 300 lines are split into **6 sections of 50 lines each**. Every section has the same internal shape: a banner on its first line, 48 numbered notes, and a footer on its 50th line.

**Section 1 — Prologue (lines 001–050)**
Line 001 is the banner: `=== Section 1: Prologue — file header and provenance notes ===`. Lines 002–049 are `Prologue note 01 of 48` through `note 48 of 48`. Line 050 closes it with `--- end of section 1 (Prologue) ---`. This is the slot where a real module would carry its docstring-adjacent material: what the file is, who owns it, licence, why it exists.

**Section 2 — Data model (lines 051–100)**
Banner on 051, notes 01–48 on 052–099, footer on 100. Reserved for the shapes the module would operate on — record definitions, field types, invariants, which fields are optional.

**Section 3 — Control flow (lines 101–150)**
Banner on 101, notes on 102–149, footer on 150. The order things happen in: entry point, the main loop, branch conditions, where state is mutated.

**Section 4 — Error handling (lines 151–200)**
Banner on 151, notes on 152–199, footer on 200. What can go wrong and the response: which exceptions are raised versus swallowed, retry policy, what gets logged.

**Section 5 — Performance (lines 201–250)**
Banner on 201, notes on 202–249, footer on 250. Cost notes — allocations, hot paths, complexity of the inner loop, anything worth caching.

**Section 6 — Epilogue (lines 251–300)**
Banner on 251, notes on 252–299, footer on 300 (`--- end of section 6 (Epilogue) ---`, the last line of the file). Open questions and follow-up work.

The arithmetic that generates it: for line `i`, the section index is `(i-1) // 50` and the position within the section is `(i-1) % 50 + 1` — position 1 gets the banner, position 50 the footer, and everything between is numbered `pos - 1`, which is why the notes run 01–48 rather than starting at the line number.
